name: systemd
summary: A system and service manager that models boot and runtime work as typed units, dependency transactions, supervised services, activation triggers, cgroup resource hierarchies, structured journals, and configurable execution boundaries.

features.name: Typed unit model
features.description: systemd represents services, sockets, mounts, devices, targets, timers, slices, and scopes as typed units loaded from unit files and managed through a common state model.
benefits: Provides one lifecycle abstraction across system resources
Makes configuration and relationships inspectable
costs: Unit type semantics and default dependencies create a large configuration surface
Misconfiguration can affect boot and service availability

features.name: Dependency transaction graph
features.description: Unit requirements and ordering directives form transactions in which systemd pulls in dependencies, orders jobs, and resolves conflicts before executing lifecycle operations.
benefits: Coordinates complex startup and shutdown relationships
Separates requirement relationships from ordering relationships
costs: Graph composition and conflicting jobs are operationally complex
Dependency success does not by itself guarantee service readiness

features.name: Supervised service lifecycle
features.description: systemd starts and tracks service processes, supports explicit readiness protocols such as notify, applies timeouts and watchdogs, and can restart services according to exit outcomes.
benefits: Makes process supervision and failure recovery explicit
Supports readiness-aware ordering and socket activation
costs: Service behavior must conform to selected supervision protocol
Restart and timeout policies can amplify resource pressure

features.name: Activation trigger units
features.description: Socket units listen on IPC or network endpoints and queue their associated service on activity; timer units schedule a configured unit from monotonic or calendar expressions; path units monitor filesystem conditions through inotify and queue a configured unit when those conditions become true.
benefits: Defers service process creation until an external event or schedule requires it
Uses typed trigger units with explicit ordering and rate-limit behavior
costs: Triggered services must implement the corresponding socket, timer, or path contract
Trigger rate limits and event semantics can turn repeated activity into unit failure

features.name: Cgroup resource hierarchy
features.description: systemd places services, sockets, scopes, and slices in a hierarchical cgroup tree and applies controller-backed accounting and limits such as CPU, memory, I/O, task, device, and network controls through unit configuration.
benefits: Provides hierarchical resource accounting and control for related units
Associates process lifetime and resource ownership with unit and slice state
costs: Effective limits depend on parent hierarchy, kernel controller support, and delegation
Controller interactions and nested slices add operational complexity

features.name: Structured journal observability
features.description: systemd-journald collects kernel, syslog, native journal, service standard-output, and audit inputs into structured indexed journals, adding trusted metadata such as process identity, unit, cgroup, boot, and invocation identifiers.
benefits: Correlates logs with unit lifecycle, process, cgroup, boot, and invocation context
Supports volatile or persistent storage and independent journal namespaces
costs: Persistence, retention, namespace, and access policy remain deployment choices
Stopping journald terminates service stream connections until affected services restart

features.name: Boot and recovery targets
features.description: The system manager composes boot and shutdown through special targets including sysinit.target, basic.target, default.target, shutdown.target, emergency.target, and rescue.target; failure to start the default target falls back to rescue.target, while emergency.target provides a minimal recovery shell.
benefits: Makes boot milestones, shutdown ordering, and recovery modes explicit in the unit graph
Allows staged recovery with either minimal emergency or basic rescue services
costs: Boot behavior depends on generated units, enabled dependencies, and target selection
Recovery targets expose powerful administrative capabilities and require careful access control

features.name: Per-unit isolation boundaries
features.description: Service execution can establish private mount, network, IPC, PID, user, and cgroup namespaces, restrict filesystem views and capabilities, and expose selected journal or credential paths through unit-specific namespace setup.
benefits: Reduces the resources and kernel-facing views visible to a service process
Makes identity, capability, filesystem, namespace, and credential policy declarative per unit
costs: Isolation settings can break services that require shared namespaces or host filesystem access
Security strength depends on kernel support and the completeness of the configured restrictions

mathematical_views.question: How do unit types, requirements, ordering edges, aliases, and drop-ins define the managed system graph?
assumptions: Unit files and generated units are the modeled configuration inputs
Requirement and ordering edges remain distinct

mathematical_views.question: How do queued jobs move units through activation, running, failure, reload, and shutdown states?
assumptions: A transaction may be changed to resolve conflicts
Runtime state can be reloaded while preserving selected service state

mathematical_views.question: Under what service outcomes does systemd declare readiness, failure, timeout, or restart?
assumptions: Readiness depends on the configured service type
Restart behavior is policy-dependent and rate-limited

mathematical_views.question: How do socket, timer, and path units add event-triggered edges and rate limits to the unit dependency graph?
assumptions: Trigger units and their configured target units are modeled as typed graph nodes
Implicit ordering and explicit requirement edges remain distinct

mathematical_views.question: How do slices, scopes, services, and cgroup controllers distribute accounting and resource constraints through a unit hierarchy?
assumptions: The cgroup tree and controller settings are the modeled resource state
Parent and delegated-controller effects are represented as inherited constraints

mathematical_views.question: How do special targets and manager crash/reboot policies move the system between initialization, normal operation, shutdown, and recovery states?
assumptions: Special targets are synchronization and transition states rather than a complete boot proof
Generated units and deployment-specific target dependencies are external inputs

mathematical_views.question: Which process, filesystem, namespace, capability, credential, and cgroup boundaries are established for a configured service unit?
assumptions: The unit execution context and namespace mount plan are the modeled boundary inputs
Kernel and container-manager support limits the effective boundary
